title: The Bird Looks Back
summary: Tutorial: learn to move, talk, find story pieces, open the Codex and run between places. Sample content.

nodes.speaker: Narrator
nodes.text: Welcome to Sankofa Trails! Move with the arrow keys or WASD (on a phone, use the pad). Glowing stars mark objects: walk up and press E (or tap Talk) to read a story piece. Then talk to the Elder the same way.

nodes.speaker: Narrator
nodes.text: You step into a quiet courtyard. Above the doorway sits a carved bird. Its feet face forward, but its head is turned to look backward.

nodes.speaker: Elder
nodes.text: Welcome, traveller. Tell me, why do you think the bird looks back?

nodes.prompt: Why does the bird look back?

options.outcome: A fair guess. But the carving is telling a different story.

options.text: To remember what it left behind.
options.outcome: Yes. That is exactly the idea behind this symbol.

nodes.title: Sankofa
nodes.text: Sankofa is a word from the Akan language of Ghana. It is often shown as a bird that looks backward while its feet face forward. It carries the idea that we can return to the past to learn what we need for the future.

nodes.speaker: Elder
nodes.text: Keep that in mind as we walk on. The road to the next place must be run: press Space to jump, and press again in the air to double jump over tall trees.

items.title: Clay pots
items.text: Clay pots like these have been made in West Africa for thousands of years to carry water and store grain. Many are decorated with patterns.

items.title: A drum
items.text: Drums are used across West Africa for music, dance and ceremony. Some can even imitate the rise and fall of speech, to send messages far away.

nodes.speaker: Narrator
nodes.text: Tip: open the Menu (or press Esc) and choose Codex to read the entries you have unlocked. A new entry appears each time you learn something important.

nodes.speaker: Elder
nodes.text: Look at the wall behind me. Every pattern on it is a symbol with a meaning.

nodes.prompt: What would you like to learn about first?

options.outcome: We will come to that. First, the symbols themselves.

nodes.title: Adinkra
nodes.text: Adinkra are visual symbols associated with the Akan peoples of West Africa. Each symbol stands for an idea or a proverb. They appear on cloth, pottery, walls and many other things.

nodes.speaker: Elder
nodes.text: Come, there is one more place I want to show you.

items.title: Grain basket
items.text: Woven baskets are made from grasses and palm fibres in many African communities. They are used to carry, store and sort food.

items.title: Mortar and pestle
items.text: Pounding grain in a wooden mortar with a pestle is an everyday task in many places in Africa. The pestle can be as tall as a person.

nodes.speaker: Elder
nodes.text: These ideas travelled with people across a whole country. Let me tell you where we are.

nodes.title: Ghana
nodes.text: Ghana is a country in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea. Its capital is Accra. The Akan language family, which includes Twi and Fante, is widely spoken there.

nodes.speaker: Elder
nodes.text: That is the end of this sample trail. Well walked.

items.title: The signpost
items.text: A signpost shows where you have been and where you are going. Sankofa asks us to look back as well as forward.

items.title: Campfire
items.text: In many communities, evening fires are a place for stories. Elders tell tales and histories to the young around the flames.
